title: Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria (RSD) and ADHD
summary: Rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD) can make criticism feel unbearable. Learn what RSD is, how it links to ADHD, and what can help.
body_markdown:
Rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD) describes an intense, fast emotional reaction to real or perceived rejection, criticism, or failure. Clinicians most often use the term with people who have ADHD, who may experience difficulty in regulating their emotions. RSD is a widely used clinical descriptor but it does not appear in the[DSM-5-TR](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/book/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425787) , the manual U.S. clinicians use for mental health diagnoses.


According to a[2024 CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7340a1.htm) , About 15.5 million U.S. adults, or 6.0%, report a current ADHD diagnosis. If you’ve just heard the term rejection sensitive dysphoria and felt a jolt of recognition in your own behaviors, you’re not alone. Many people spend years feeling that small comments affect them more than it does other people, with no understanding for why.


## Rejection sensitive dysphoria at a glance


- **What it is:** An intense emotional reaction to real or perceived rejection, criticism, or failure
- **Diagnostic status:** A clinical descriptor used in ADHD care. It does not appear in the DSM-5-TR
- **Main link to ADHD** : An experience often described by people with ADHD, where emotion dysregulation is common
- **How it can feel:** Sudden emotional pain, often with physical sensations like nausea or chest tightness
- **What can help:** Coping strategies, therapy, and ADHD treatment, guided by a comprehensive evaluation


## How RSD differs from everyday hurt feelings


People without ADHD may wonder how RSD differs from the usual sting everyone feels after criticism. After all, negative words and comments can make anyone feel bad, and you don’t need a mental health condition to explain it.


But the difference between RSD and everyday hurt feelings comes down to the size of the negative effect, the speed, and staying power of the reaction.


Picture a coworker answering your idea with a one-word “fine.” Everyday hurt feelings might bring a flicker of doubt that fades by lunch. With RSD, that same reply can set off a wave of shame that feels far out of proportion, and it may last all day or longer.


Everyday hurt feelings Rejection sensitive dysphoria (as commonly described)


What sets it off Clear, significant criticism or rejection Small or ambiguous cues, including rejection that may not have happened


Speed Tends to build gradually Often hits within moments


Intensity Uncomfortable but manageable Overwhelming, sometimes felt as physical pain


How long it lasts Usually fades as the situation resolves Can last hours or longer, and memories can resurface years later


Effect on behavior May prompt reflection or a conversation Can lead to withdrawal, people pleasing, or avoiding risks


Note that these descriptions come from clinical accounts and qualitative research. They are not formal diagnostic criteria.


Now that you know how RSD reaction differs, it helps to know where the name came from and what its status actually means.


## RSD meaning: where the term comes from


The term RSD is much younger than the experience it describes, and it came out of ADHD clinical practice.[Psychiatrist William Dodson, MD, is widely credited with coining the term](https://chadd.org/adhd-weekly/rejection-can-more-painful-with-adhd/) and he describes RSD as an often-overlooked part of adult ADHD.


Many people now first hear about RSD on social media, long before they raise it with a provider. “Dysphoria” comes from a Greek word meaning hard to bear, and in medicine it describes a state of deep emotional unease. Put together, the term names emotional pain that is hard to bear and is set off by rejection.


Because RSD does not appear in the DSM-5-TR and has no formal criteria, some readers wonder if that makes the experience less real. It doesn’t. Patients’ descriptions of RSD are detailed and consistent, and the next section walks through what an episode can feel like from start to finish.


## RSD symptoms: what an episode feels like


Most of what’s known about RSD symptoms comes from people describing their own episodes. One source is a qualitative study of university students with ADHD published in[PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0314669) .


### How an RSD episode starts


An RSD episode usually starts with a sense that someone is disappointed in you, has rejected you, or is about to. Common triggers include criticism (even when it’s gentle or constructive), a delayed reply to a text, a neutral facial expression, falling short of your own standards, or being left out of plans. Some people with RSD said that the expectation of rejection could feel worse than the rejection itself.


### How an RSD episode feels in the body


RSD tends to arrive fast and hit hard. Participants described rejection as a full-body experience, with nausea, chest tightness, and a sense of burning or freezing.


Others compared it to a pinch in the chest, a closing throat, or the feeling of the floor dropping away. There is often little time to think before the feeling takes over, which can make the reaction feel out of your control.


### How long an RSD episode lasts


The length of an RSD episode varies a lot. Some people with RSD said an episode could last anywhere from hours to weeks. Some said a painful memory of rejection could resurface years later with much of its original force.


Because people’s experience with RSD differs so much, keeping track of your own experiences and reactions can help a provider understand what you’re dealing with.


### What an RSD episode looks like to others


Your friends and coworkers will only ever see a small part of an RSD episode from the outside. They might notice you going silent, leaving early, snapping at a mild comment, or tearing up suddenly.


People with ADHD and RSD tend to hide the reactions as well. The PLOS ONE participants described wearing a “mask of toughness,” which often left them feeling disconnected and alone.


Episodes this intense raise a fair question: why does rejection hit this hard? For many people, ADHD is a big part of the answer.


## ADHD can make rejection feel more intense


ADHD can make rejection feel more intense mainly because ADHD often comes with emotion dysregulation. That means trouble managing the size, speed, and length of emotional reactions.


### Emotion dysregulation makes reactions rise faster and higher


A major review in the American Journal of Psychiatry found that[emotion dysregulation is a common experience in ADHD at every age and can add to daily difficulties](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24480998/) .


Adults with ADHD reported much more emotion dysregulation than adults without ADHD. When emotions rise faster and higher, a minor slight can feel like a major one.


### ADHD may change how the brain handles emotional signals


Researchers don’t know yet exactly why ADHD and RSD so often appear together. One theory is that ADHD may affect how the brain notices, recognizes, and directs attention to emotional signals, which could make it harder to step back from a painful feeling once it starts.


### Years of correction can make criticism feel heavier


Many people who struggle with ADHD grow up being corrected by parents, teachers, and friends when they behave in ways that aren’t perceived as normal or acceptable. Maybe you’ve been chastised or criticized for forgetting things or missing details.


Some clinicians believe that years of that kind of feedback can make each new criticism feel heavier. RSD comes up often in conversations about how ADHD presents in women, who are frequently diagnosed later in life.


ADHD is a common reason that rejection can feel more painful, but several other conditions can produce reactions that look a lot like RSD, which is why getting the right evaluation matters.


## Telling RSD apart from similar conditions


Intense reactions to rejection can happen without ADHD, and some people have more than one condition at once.


A comprehensive evaluation is the most reliable way to tell RSD apart from conditions that look similar.


Condition What it can share with RSD Clues a provider may use to tell them apart


Social anxiety Fear of judgment and avoiding social situations Worry that tends to build before social events, not only after a perceived slight


Complex trauma (complex PTSD) Strong reactions to cues of criticism or abandonment A history of long-term or repeated trauma, plus symptoms like flashbacks


Depression Low mood and harsh self-criticism after setbacks Low mood that lasts for weeks, whether or not anything upsetting happened


Borderline personality disorder (BPD) Intense emotional reactions in close relationships How long emotions take to settle and how many areas of life are affected


### Why BPD calls for particular care


Clinicians take particular care in telling ADHD-related emotion dysregulation apart from BPD.[Emotional reactions in BPD tend to last longer and return to baseline more slowly](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40479-018-0086-8) . A trained clinician and a thorough evaluation is needed to tell these differences in experience and conditions apart.


### How a provider tells these conditions apart


A provider will often ask you how long your reactions last, what sets them off, and how they affect your daily life. They may also ask about your ability to focus during your childhood, your moods, and any history of trauma.


Before your appointment, jot down two or three recent moments when you had a reaction that felt bigger than the situation called for. Concrete examples give a provider more to work with than a general description.

If your reactions to rejection are affecting your daily life, speaking with a primary care provider can help.


Whatever the source, these big negative reactions rarely stay contained to one moment. They tend to follow you into your closest relationships and your job, which is where many people struggle most.


## How RSD affects relationships and work


RSD’s effects tend to show up first with the people you see most, at home and at work.


In relationships, RSD can turn small moments into painful ones. A partner’s tired tone or a friend’s slow reply may feel like proof of rejection. Some people respond by pulling away, while others work hard to keep everyone happy. Our[guide to relationships and Mental Health](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/mental-health-and-relationships) goes deeper into these challenges.


At work, feedback is often where RSD can get triggered. A routine performance review can feel crushing, and some people avoid applying for promotions to escape the risk of hearing criticism. Over time, constant effort to avoid criticism can wear you down and may contribute to ADHD burnout.


Effects like these are usually what push people to look for help. The good news is that RSD can be managed both on your own and with a provider.


## How to manage rejection sensitive dysphoria


Managing rejection sensitive dysphoria usually works on two levels. Coping strategies help you get through an episode, and treatment guided by a provider can address what’s driving your reactions.


### Coping strategies for RSD episodes


These coping strategies won’t stop RSD every episode, but many people find they shorten or soften a negative reaction to rejection


1. **Name the reaction as it happens.** Telling yourself “this is RSD” can create a little distance from the feeling.
2. **Pause before you reply.** Wait at least an hour before answering a message that stung.
3. **Separate the facts from the feeling.** Write down what was said, then write down what you felt it meant.
4. **Plan a recovery step in advance.** Pick a walk, a song, or a call to a friend you can turn to quickly.
5. **Tell people you trust what helps.** A simple heads-up like “direct feedback works better for me in writing” can prevent negative feelings from escalating.
6. **Notice when you’re hiding.** RSD can drive ADHD masking, so watch for times you perform calm instead of feeling it.


### Treatment approaches that can help with RSD


Talk therapy, including cognitive behavioral approaches and therapies that build emotion regulation skills, can help people respond to perceived rejection differently.


Treating underlying ADHD may also reduce emotion dysregulation for some people.[Circle Medical offers ADHD evaluation and treatment](https://www.circlemedical.com/what-we-treat/adhd) from the comfort of your home.


Results may vary, and treatment isn’t a guaranteed fix for RSD. When clinically appropriate, a provider can build a personalized treatment plan tailored to your needs.


## Common questions about rejection sensitive dysphoria


### What does rejection sensitive dysphoria feel like?


People with rejection sensitive dysphoria often describe sudden, intense emotional pain after criticism or perceived rejection. Many feel it physically, through nausea, chest tightness, or a burning or frozen sensation. The reaction usually feels far bigger than the event that caused it.


### What does an RSD episode look like?


An RSD episode can look like withdrawal, tears, anger, or sudden silence after a minor comment. Some people hide the reaction completely and seem fine on the outside. Episodes can last from hours to weeks, and some people replay the moment long afterward.


### What causes rejection sensitive dysphoria?


The exact cause of RSD isn’t known. Researchers link it to emotion dysregulation, which is common in ADHD and may involve how the brain processes emotional signals. Frequent criticism in childhood may also play a part. Other conditions, including anxiety and trauma, can produce similar reactions.


### How can I manage RSD?


Many people manage RSD with a mix of coping strategies and clinical care. Helpful habits include naming the reaction, pausing before responding, and separating facts from feelings. Therapy can build emotion regulation skills, and treating underlying ADHD may help. A provider can help you decide which options fit your situation.


### Is RSD an official diagnosis?


Rejection sensitive dysphoria does not appear in the DSM-5-TR as a diagnosis. RSD is a widely used clinical descriptor, mostly in ADHD care. The experience is real and well described by patients, even though formal criteria haven’t been developed.


### Can you have RSD without ADHD?


Yes, strong reactions to rejection can occur without ADHD. Because RSD isn’t a formal diagnosis, similar experiences can come from social anxiety, depression, complex trauma, or other mental health conditions. A comprehensive evaluation can help a provider understand what’s behind your reactions.


### Is RSD the same as being oversensitive?


RSD differs from general sensitivity in its intensity and speed. Everyday hurt feelings stay manageable and fade as the situation resolves. With RSD, the reaction can be overwhelming, arrive within moments, and last much longer. Calling it oversensitivity can add shame to an already painful experience.


### Does ADHD medication help with RSD?


ADHD treatment may reduce emotion dysregulation for some people, according to a review in the American Journal of Psychiatry. That can make reactions to rejection feel more manageable. No medication is approved specifically for RSD, and results vary. A provider can discuss whether treatment is clinically appropriate for you.


## Book an ADHD consultation today


Being able to name RSD for what you’re experiencing can bring real relief. That’s a starting point for care. But knowing that the same large reactions you have against criticism can come from ADHD, anxiety, trauma, or a mix of them. A consultation helps you find out which is really involved.

2. A comprehensive health assessment of about 30 minutes

Follow-up visits then track how you’re doing. Bring your notes on recent RSD episodes, since they turn a hard-to-describe feeling into something you and your provider can work on together.
